patient.chief_complaint: Acute left-sided vision loss with headache for 5 days
patient.history_present_illness: Ms. Lucia Vega is a 29-year-old right-handed Hispanic woman who presents to the emergency department with a five-day history of progressive left-sided visual field loss. She reports that she first noticed difficulty seeing objects to her left while driving home from work five days ago, initially thinking her glasses were smudged. Over the next 24 hours, the visual deficit became more pronounced and she began having difficulty reading text on her computer screen, missing words on the left side of the page. She also developed a bifrontal headache that she describes as a constant dull pressure, rated 5 out of 10 in severity, which is different in character from her typical migraines. The headache has been accompanied by mild photophobia and intermittent floaters in the left eye. She denies any associated nausea, vomiting, or phonophobia. She has no history of similar visual symptoms. She reports that approximately fifteen months ago she experienced a two-week episode of numbness and tingling involving the right side of her face and right arm that resolved spontaneously. She attributed this to work-related stress and did not seek medical evaluation at the time. She denies any recent head trauma, fevers, chills, weight loss, joint pains, oral ulcers, or skin rashes. She denies any recent travel or sick contacts. Her primary care physician referred her to the emergency department after an urgent noncontrast CT scan of the head showed a hypodense area in the right parieto-occipital region with surrounding edema, raising concern for acute ischemia versus a mass lesion. Given her age and the acute presentation, she was admitted for further workup. On review of systems, she endorses mild fatigue over the past several months but denies any limb weakness, difficulty walking, urinary or bowel dysfunction, or swallowing difficulties. Her family history is notable for autoimmune disease in her mother, which has raised concern for a possible autoimmune etiology.

results.title: Tumefactive demyelination: clinical, radiological, and prognostic features
results.authors: Lucchinetti CF, Gavrilova RH, Metz I, et al.
results.key_finding: Tumefactive demyelinating lesions (>2 cm) can mimic neoplasm or abscess. Open ring enhancement pattern is a key differentiator. Most patients respond to high-dose IV corticosteroids. Approximately two-thirds of patients with tumefactive demyelination are ultimately diagnosed with MS.

results.title: Tumefactive multiple sclerosis: a rare presentation requiring differentiation from CNS neoplasm
results.authors: Hardy TA, Reddel SW, Barnett MH, et al.
results.key_finding: IV methylprednisolone (1 g daily for 5 days) is first-line treatment. Plasmapheresis or IVIG may be considered in steroid-refractory cases. Brain biopsy should be reserved for cases where imaging and laboratory findings are inconclusive. Most tumefactive MS patients transition to typical RRMS and require disease-modifying therapy.

results.title: Distinguishing tumefactive demyelination from glioma: role of MR spectroscopy and perfusion imaging
results.authors: Kiriyama T, Kataoka H, Ueno S, et al.
results.key_finding: MR spectroscopy in tumefactive demyelination shows mildly elevated choline and reduced NAA with lactate peak, whereas gliomas show markedly elevated choline (Cho/Cr >2.0). Perfusion imaging shows lower cerebral blood volume in demyelinating lesions compared to gliomas.

output.summary: Tumefactive demyelinating lesions (>2 cm with mass effect and edema) are an uncommon presentation of MS that can mimic brain tumors. Key imaging discriminators include the open ring enhancement pattern and MR spectroscopy features. High-dose corticosteroids have been used in acute management; brain biopsy may be necessary if noninvasive workup is inconclusive. Approximately two-thirds of patients with tumefactive demyelination are eventually diagnosed with relapsing-remitting MS.

differential.key_features: Homogeneous enhancement (often without open ring), periventricular location, restricted diffusion, marked steroid sensitivity; consider in immunocompromised hosts — distinguish by biopsy if imaging is equivocal
Closed-ring enhancement (rather than open ring with cortical-side break), elevated choline:NAA on spectroscopy, lack of CSF oligoclonal bands; tissue diagnosis often required
AQP4-IgG positivity, longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis, area postrema syndrome — must be excluded before DMT selection
MOG-IgG positivity, ADEM-like large lesions especially in younger patients, frequent lesion resolution on follow-up MRI
Restricted diffusion centrally (not peripheral), thick smooth ring, fever and elevated inflammatory markers, predisposing source (dental, sinus, endocarditis)
Monophasic, post-infectious/post-vaccination, encephalopathy hallmark; large confluent lesions; MOG-IgG sometimes positive in young adults

optimal_actions.action: Obtain contrast-enhanced brain MRI with MS protocol (FLAIR, T2, DWI, pre- and post-gadolinium T1) to assess dissemination in space and time
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Multifocal T2/FLAIR hyperintensities in MS-typical regions (periventricular, juxtacortical/cortical, infratentorial); presence of gadolinium-enhancing lesion(s) supports dissemination in time when also non-enhancing lesions present

optimal_actions.action: Extend MRI to cervical and thoracic spinal cord with contrast — ~80% of MS patients have cord lesions, and cord involvement counts toward dissemination in space
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Short-segment (<2 vertebral bodies) peripheral cord lesions favor MS over NMOSD (which characteristically shows longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis ≥3 segments)

optimal_actions.action: Perform lumbar puncture for CSF analysis including oligoclonal bands (paired serum), IgG index, cell count, protein, and glucose
optimal_actions.expected_finding: CSF-restricted oligoclonal bands (≥2) and/or elevated IgG index support inflammatory CNS demyelination; per McDonald 2017 OCBs can substitute for dissemination in time in CIS with DIS

useless_tools.rationale: EEG has no role in MS diagnosis — findings are non-specific and do not contribute to dissemination in space or time.
CT is markedly inferior to MRI for visualising demyelinating plaques; ordering CT delays diagnosis and adds radiation without clinical benefit.
No cardiac indication in a typical MS workup; echocardiography does not inform the demyelinating differential.
Cardiac monitoring is only indicated for first-dose fingolimod initiation (bradyarrhythmia risk) — not as part of MS diagnostic workup.
FDG-PET is not indicated for MS diagnosis or DMT decisions; it does not differentiate demyelination from mimics and adds substantial cost.

sequence_constraints.reason: Standard pre-LP imaging: confirm absence of mass effect / herniation risk on brain MRI before lumbar puncture

critical_actions: Establish dissemination in space (DIS) using brain and spinal-cord MRI in MS-typical regions (periventricular, juxtacortical/cortical, infratentorial, spinal cord)
Establish dissemination in time (DIT) by demonstrating simultaneous enhancing and non-enhancing lesions, a new lesion on follow-up MRI, or CSF-restricted oligoclonal bands (per McDonald 2017)
Exclude NMOSD and MOGAD with AQP4-IgG and MOG-IgG cell-based assays before committing to an MS diagnosis and DMT
Order CSF analysis with paired serum to assess oligoclonal bands and IgG index
For tumefactive presentations with mass effect, consult neurosurgery and consider brain biopsy if imaging plus CSF/serology do not establish diagnosis with confidence
Treat the acute relapse with high-dose IV methylprednisolone (1 g daily for 3–5 days), with plasma exchange reserved for steroid-refractory severe relapses
Initiate a disease-modifying therapy (DMT) after relapse stabilization; choice between platform vs. high-efficacy agent based on disease activity, MRI burden, and patient preference
Check JC virus antibody serostatus before considering natalizumab; verify up-to-date vaccinations (especially live-attenuated) before initiating B-cell depleting or S1P-modulator DMTs
Counsel on Uhthoff phenomenon, heat avoidance, smoking cessation, and vitamin D supplementation as modifiable lifestyle factors
contraindicated_actions: Do not diagnose MS based on non-specific white-matter lesions alone without meeting McDonald 2017 criteria and excluding mimics
Do not start natalizumab in a JC virus-antibody-positive patient (especially with high index) without explicit benefit-risk discussion of PML
Do not initiate fingolimod without a baseline ECG and first-dose bradyarrhythmia monitoring; avoid in patients with second-degree AV block, prior MI, or severe sleep apnea
Do not start teriflunomide in a woman of child-bearing potential without effective contraception (teratogenic, long elimination half-life)
Do not use chronic oral corticosteroids as a maintenance treatment for MS — they are ineffective long-term and carry significant harm
Do not administer live-attenuated vaccines after initiation of B-cell depleting therapy (ocrelizumab, ofatumumab) or S1P modulators (fingolimod, ozanimod)
Do not omit spinal-cord MRI in a patient with myelopathic signs even if the brain MRI alone meets DIS criteria — cord lesions change relapse counting and management

Do not pursue aggressive cytoreductive surgery for a presumed tumefactive demyelinating lesion before exhausting non-invasive workup — open ring enhancement, CSF OCBs, and AQP4/MOG serology should be obtained first
key_reasoning_points: MS is a clinical-radiographic diagnosis: McDonald 2017 requires dissemination in space (DIS) and dissemination in time (DIT) plus exclusion of better explanations — no single test confirms it

MS-typical MRI regions are periventricular, juxtacortical/cortical, infratentorial, and spinal cord — recognising a lesion in three of these regions establishes DIS for an attack-meeting clinical event
CSF-restricted oligoclonal bands (≥2 bands not present in paired serum) can substitute for DIT under McDonald 2017 when DIS is met — this changes the calculus for clinically isolated syndromes

Short-segment (<2 vertebral bodies), peripheral, dorsolateral or dorsal-column spinal cord lesions strongly favour MS over NMOSD (which characteristically produces longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis ≥3 segments)

Tumefactive demyelinating lesions are a recognised MS variant — distinguishing imaging features from neoplasm include open ring enhancement, prominent intralesional venules, less mass effect than expected for size, and CSF OCBs; brain biopsy should be a last resort
Open-ring enhancement with the opening oriented toward the cortex is a high-specificity sign of demyelination, distinguishing tumefactive MS from neoplasm and abscess
AQP4-IgG and MOG-IgG must be ordered as cell-based assays, not ELISA — the older ELISA-based AQP4 assays have unacceptable false-negative rates
T1 hypointense 'black holes' indicate axonal loss from prior inflammatory episodes and contribute evidence of dissemination in time even without simultaneous enhancing lesions

Choice of DMT — platform agent (interferon-β, glatiramer, teriflunomide, dimethyl fumarate) vs. high-efficacy agent (natalizumab, ocrelizumab, ofatumumab, cladribine, S1P modulators) — should weigh disease activity, MRI burden, patient comorbidities, JCV serostatus, and reproductive plans
If the initial brain MRI does not include the spinal cord, extending imaging to cervical and thoracic cord is essential — both for diagnostic DIS and for relapse counting
Low serum vitamin D is a known MS risk factor and a modifiable comorbidity; while it is NOT a diagnostic criterion, supplementation is part of comprehensive management

A low-titre ANA (1:40 or 1:80 without specific extractable nuclear antigen positivity) is common in the general population and does not establish a connective-tissue mimic — do not over-call CNS lupus or undifferentiated connective tissue disease on this alone

red_herrings.intended_effect: May tempt the agent to attribute the patient's neurological symptoms to vitamin D deficiency or to label this as a 'metabolic' presentation
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Low vitamin D is a recognised MS risk factor and a modifiable comorbidity, NOT a diagnostic criterion — it should be supplemented but does not change or explain the MS workup

red_herrings.intended_effect: May suggest CNS lupus, undifferentiated connective tissue disease, or another autoimmune mimic
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Low-titre ANA (1:40–1:80) without specific extractable nuclear antigen positivity is common in healthy young women and does not establish a connective-tissue mimic of MS

metadata.difficulty_description: Moderate — tumefactive demyelinating lesion mimicking a brain tumor on initial imaging, with a positive ANA and family history of SLE serving as red herrings. The agent must recognize the open ring enhancement pattern as characteristic of demyelination, exclude neoplasm and CNS lupus through CSF and antibody testing, and identify a prior subclinical demyelinating episode to establish MS diagnosis. The initial CT interpretation suggesting stroke adds an additional layer of diagnostic misdirection.
clinical_pearls: Open ring enhancement, where the non-enhancing portion faces the cortex (gray matter), has >90% specificity for demyelinating lesions and is the key imaging discriminator from neoplasm

Tumefactive demyelinating lesions (>2 cm) are uncommon presentations of MS that can closely mimic brain tumors; approximately two-thirds of patients with tumefactive demyelination are eventually diagnosed with RRMS

A positive ANA alone is insufficient to diagnose CNS lupus — lupus-specific antibodies (anti-dsDNA, anti-Smith) must be tested, particularly when the clinical and imaging findings point to an alternative diagnosis

MR spectroscopy can help differentiate demyelination from high-grade glioma: demyelination shows mildly elevated choline (Cho/Cr ~1.2-1.5) whereas gliomas typically show markedly elevated choline (Cho/Cr >2.0)
Patients presenting with tumefactive MS should be considered for high-efficacy disease-modifying therapy given the aggressive disease phenotype
metadata.difficulty_rationale: Tumefactive demyelinating lesion overlaps imaging features with neoplasm/abscess; differential must include CNS lymphoma and high-grade glioma; agent must integrate open-ring enhancement, CSF OCB status, and AQP4/MOG serology to avoid biopsy
